To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

partisans exaggerate the extent to which their own opinions differ with those of their rivals, and it is the perception of disagreement about the partisan's own core values that predicts the partisan's global evaluation of the rival group.

partisans exaggerate how much disagreement there is with the rival group on the issues that are central to the partisan's own position, that this perception of disagreement predicts partisans' evaluations of the rival group, and that this perception of the rival group as motivated to oppose the partisans' position rather than promote its own position is a key factor in the perception of disagreement.

members of partisan social groups (a) exaggerate how much they disagree with their rivals about issues that are important to their own group, but (b) underestimate how much they disagree about issues that are central to the rival group, and (c) perceive that their adversaries are motivated by a negative opposition to the partisanship of the partisans' group, rather than by a positive commitment to the values of the adversary group.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the origins of intergroup conflict.
how partisans perceive the values that are central or peripheral to their rivals' ideological position and with the consequences of these perceptions for the partisans' attitudes toward the outgroup.
how the nature and content of intergroup conflict shapes the way people perceive and think about their adversaries and the conflict.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
people tend to exaggerate how much they disagree with their adversaries and to attribute their adversaries' disagreement to their own values rather than their adversaries' values.
the more central a value is to one's own group's ideology, the more one will believe one's opponents are motivated by a rejection of that value, and the more one will dislike them.

the partisans' perceptions of disagreement are driven by the partisans' desire to protect their own core values, and this desire is what motivates the partisans to misperceive the adversaries' motives.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
partisans' perceptions of disagreement are shaped by their own values and that these perceptions are what drives intergroup mistrust.
the partisans' perception of disagreement with their rivals is driven by the partisans' perceptions of their own core values and the perceived opposition to these core values by the rivals.
partisans' perceptions of the conflict are distorted in a way that is consistent with their own partisan identity.
The main takeaway from our work is that

partisans tend to misperceive their rivals' attitudes in a manner that makes them seem more extreme than they really are, and this misperception is driven by a desire to see their rivals as motivated by a rejection of the partisans' core values rather than a promotion of the rivals' own core values.
partisans' perceptions of the conflict and the outgroup may not be based on an accurate assessment of the situation.
people's perceptions of their rivals' attitudes are driven more by their own group's ideology than by the rivals' actual ideology.
